newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Elections worried investors in Oct.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Elections worried investors in Oct.

text.p: Anxious about the outcome of U.S. elections, mutual fund investors lost their appetite for stock funds in October, but appear this month to be hungry again, according to industry analysts.
More conservative funds, such as index and growth and income, led the pack, while more speculative funds such as growth and aggressive growth were laggards, analysts said.
"People stopped putting money into equity funds before the election," said Charles Biderman, president of Trim Tabs Financial Services, which tracks funds.
"A week and a half before the election, inflows slowed to a $300 million daily rate," Biderman said. "Three days after the election, they spiked to $2 billion a day."
"Investors were afraid that Democrats would sweep the elections, and create a tax-and-spend situation," said Biderman. "They like deadlock in Washington."

New cash flows into U.S. stock mutual funds dropped to $13 billion in October from $17.4 billion net inflow in September, according to a preliminary estimate by the Investment Company Institute, an industry trade group.
Some fund companies mirrored the decline. Charles Schwab Corp said equity fund net inflows halved to about $764 million in October, compared with $1.49 billion in September.
Inflows for aggressive growth funds shrank to $6 million in October from $495 million in September, Schwab said.
Scudder, Stevens & Clark Inc said it experienced a "moderation in inflows in October."

A Scudder spokesman said inflows for domestic equity funds dropped to $67 million in October from $130 million in September. The sector was rebounding in November. Through Nov 12, flows topped $43 million.

"People had pre-election caution, and chose to postpone some of their discretionary investment activity until after the elections," a Scudder spokesman said. "As soon as the election returns were in, there was a very significant acceleration."
T. Rowe Price Associates Inc found that October "was a good month for equities, but not quite as strong as September," according to a spokesman.
The more conservative equity income fund dominated monthly activity, while small-cap international funds "tended to be less popular," the spokesman said.
Vanguard Group said it posted total net cash inflow of $2.7 billion in October, up from $2.3 billion in September.
"We've been in the $2.3 billion to $2.8 billion range for the last six months," a spokesman said.

Equity funds posted inflows of $1.7 billion for October versus $1.5 billion in September; money market funds had flows of $600 million versus $350 million, and bond funds had $300 million versus $300 million.
Some analysts noted that the preliminary October figures were rosier than the $9.16 billion flows in October 1995.

"I would not look at this as a decline, particularly because the flow of money has just been incredible," said Burt Berry, president of DAL Investment Co. "It has a lot to do with retirement plans getting bigger."
Early returns from November suggest that investors have moved back strongly into stock funds.
"We're currently seeing a bounce back to the $15 billion to $20 billion monthly rate we saw in August and September," said Biderman.
-- Mutual fund desk, 212-859-1735.
